articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: This Gamescom Showcase Did A Lot Of Games Dirty
articles.subtitle: It’s hard to criticize Gamescom’s Opening Night Live showcase without accidentally firing off shots at games that probably don’t deserve it, but that was a pretty miserable showcase.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
It’s hard to criticize Gamescom’s Opening Night Live showcase without accidentally firing off shots at games that probably don’t deserve it, but that was a pretty miserable showcase. Geoff Keighley hosts the biggest English-language video game showcases of the year, and the Germany-based presentation is typically the one that feels the least curated. This year, it also feels like the format is serving very few games on the stage.

If you were to pluck most of the trailers in the two-hour show out of the event, you probably could find a lot to be excited about. But the lineup at Gamescom hurt a lot of these games, as so many of them had such similar vibes, gameplay loops, and aesthetics that they all kind of blended together and painted a pretty stultifying picture of the months ahead.

I just wrote our recap for the showcase, and found that about midway through I was running out of things to say about every dark fantasy game, edgy shooter, or anime-inspired Hoyoverse-esque game as it came and went without a moment of impact.

Obviously, Keighley had a few major games up his sleeve to act as the headliners, but Final Fantasy VII Revelation ’s appearance was all too brief after we’d endured nearly two hours of games that couldn’t hope to meaningfully differentiate themselves from all the others.

The night’s final reveal, a remaster of The Witcher 3, was probably the biggest surprise of the show, which is kind of anticlimactic note to end on, as it’s an 11-year-old game. At least it’s getting a hefty expansion next year so there’s something new on the horizon.

This is the same struggle that shows like Wholesome Games have run into, in that they’re so curated around a specific theme that showing too many games at once runs the risk of them all bleeding into each other, and the longer the show goes on, the less time anyone gets to process something that looks cool before their short-term memory is overwritten by the next not-distinct-enough game.

This year’s Gamescom felt like the also-ran of Keighley’s shows.

Summer Game Fest has taken up E3’s usual place as the summer show that everyone pays attention to, and the Game Awards has prestige to chase as it positions itself as the video-game Oscars, which leaves Gamescom in this awkward spot of sometimes feeling like a place for Keighley and crew to dump all the miscellaneous games that aren’t quite big enough to headline one of the glitzier showcases.

And while some of these games will surely benefit from being featured here, it doesn’t do them any real favors to get overshadowed by Final Fantasy VII.

articles.title: New Mac Mini and Mac Studio: 13 Things You Might Have Missed
articles.subtitle: Apple today announced new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini models and M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio models. We've covered all of the announcements in-depth, but wanted to highlight some interesting tidbits about the new machines.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Price Increases - The Mac mini now starts at $899, $300 over the original starting price of the M4 Mac mini when it launched in October 2024. Mac Studio pricing starts at $2,499, $500 more than the original price of the M4 Max model when it came out in March 2025.

Connectivity - Apple upgraded the new Macs with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, so they are on par with the connectivity standards in the latest iPhone models. Wi-Fi 7 offers faster data speeds in the 6GHz band, lower latency, and an option to connect across 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz networks at once for reliability improvements.

Genlock - The ‌Mac mini‌ and ‌Mac Studio‌ support genlock over USB-C, so there's no need for a separate sync box. Genlock is used in multi-camera shoots and virtual production to lock timing to a shared reference signal. The Mac's display and the camera filming it are synchronized, preventing flickering and tearing from a mismatch between the display refresh rate and camera shutter.

Apple previously added genlock support to the iPhone 17 Pro models, so now an ‌iPhone 17 Pro‌ and one of the new Macs can work in tandem for pros who need the feature.

Ethernet - The ‌Mac mini‌ now starts with 2.5Gb Ethernet instead of 1Gb. There's an option to upgrade to 10Gb, which is what the ‌Mac Studio‌ starts with (same as the prior-generation model).

Neural Engine - The M6 chip has an upgraded Neural Engine with two 16-core engines instead of just one. Apple says the new Neural Engine offers 2x more peak compute so AI workflows run faster.

GPU - The M6 ‌Mac mini‌'s 12-core GPU has Neural Accelerators in each core, offering up to 4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than the ‌M4 Mac mini‌. The ‌Mac Studio‌'s M5 Ultra is also the first Ultra chip with Neural Accelerators. Peak AI compute performance is 4.3x the M3 Ultra's performance.

SSD - ‌Mac Studio‌ storage is twice as fast with new SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.

SSD Pricing - As Daring Fireball points out, upgrading a ‌Mac mini‌ with a 2TB SSD costs $1,000, which is more than the $899 base price of the machine. Upgrading to the 4TB SSD for the M5 Pro costs $1,800, which is $100 over the price of the base machine.

Thunderbolt - The M6 ‌Mac mini‌ continues to have Thunderbolt 4, not Thunderbolt 5. The M5 Pro model does have Thunderbolt 5.

Current Max Pricing - An M5 Pro ‌Mac mini‌ with 18-core CPU, 64GB RAM, an 8TB SSD, and 10GbE is $6,799. The M5 Ultra ‌Mac Studio‌ with 36-core CPU, 256GB RAM, and 16TB SSD is $18,299.

512GB RAM - You can only buy the M5 Ultra with 96GB or 256GB of RAM right now, but a 512GB option is coming in late October. Since upgrading from 96GB RAM to 256GB RAM costs $4,000, the 512GB option will likely cost at least $6,000.

Announcement Timing - This is the first time Apple has announced new Macs in August since the 27-inch iMac debuted in August 2020.

macOS Golden Gate - When the new machines launch on September 22, they will likely have macOS Golden Gate installed. The software update is probably going to come out the week of September 14.

Instagram is rolling out a new Reels editing feature called First Draft that automatically trims multiple video clips and creates a shorter starting edit for users.

First Draft appears inside Instagram’s Reels editor on iPhone. Users can record videos with Instagram’s camera or choose several existing clips from their gallery, then select First Draft to create an initial cut.

Instagram analyzes the selected footage and removes sections such as long pauses or moments it considers less useful. It then combines the remaining sections into a shorter Reel that users can continue editing before publishing.

The addition gives Instagram creators another way to reduce the time spent manually cutting long videos into shorter Reels. Instagram already includes tools for arranging clips, adding audio, voiceovers, effects and saving unfinished Reels as drafts.

articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.) Writing for...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.)

Writing for Bloomberg, well-connected leaker Mark Gurman says Apple is gearing up to unveil the first new Mac mini in almost two years. He bases this on the testimony of unnamed sources “familiar with the matter.”

The last Mac mini model, announced on October 29, 2024, featured a major redesign (it was significantly smaller than its predecessor) as well as a faster M4 chip. This machine has become extremely popular, Gurman says, for running AI applications, but the ongoing memory crunch means Apple has struggled to meet demand. The Mac mini has essentially been out of stock since the spring, with delivery times slipping into months-long waits.

That isn’t to say that Apple necessarily thinks the new model will help in this regard. Gurman acknowledges that it’s unclear “how the new model will affect wait times,” as an updated mini is unlikely to require less memory than the current one. It seems more likely that Apple simply feels it’s time for an update, and the product’s popularity has pushed it to the front of the line.

Gurman’s report is generally short on details, with little information offered regarding design (although we can guess that another redesign would be a surprise so soon after the last one) and tech specs, where he says only that models with both M5 and M6 chips have been tested. The main takeaway regards timings.

Gurman says the new Mac mini could arrive ahead of the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, which will appear in early September and likely on September 9, and even says it will likely be the last product to launch under Cook’s watch.

Cook is slated to exit the CEO seat on September 1, which (assuming Gurman’s speculation is correct) gives a window of just seven days for the Mac mini to arrive. And we can rule out most of those days because they’re unsuitable for an announcement; by far the most plausible are Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. It could launch today, in other words.

The mini is only one of the Macs getting an update this fall as part of a massive overhaul. For all the latest news and rumors, bookmark our regularly updated new Mac mini superguide.

articles.content:
Fans of the GOTY contender will soon have access to Blood and Wine and Hearts of Stone DLC

If you've spent the last 11 years holding off on purchasing The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt ' s DLC, then boy does CD Projekt Red have a surprise for you. In addition to a new (and potentially free) Remastered version of the game full of quality of life improvements, both of the GOTY contender's hefty expansions are now totally free.

Normally, The Witcher 3' s Blood and Wine DLC adds dozens of hours of gameplay for the price of $19.99. Hearts of Stone, the first expansion for the venerated RPG, offers a smaller array of content for $9.99. Taking into account the existing 16 pieces of free Witcher 3 DLC and the more recent next-gen updates, those prices were already a good deal. You can't beat free, though.

If you haven't played the DLC, timing might be tricky. While the DLC is free now, The Witcher 3 Remastered is scheduled for release on Sept. 29. It'll come with a number of improvements like upgraded visuals, with CD Projekt Red promising that Geralt has "never looked better." If you play now, you don't have to wait. Alternatively, you may want to experience the best possible version of The Witcher 3, and that's undoubtedly going to be the Remastered version.

What's new in The Witcher 3 Remastered?

The Witcher 3 Remastered adds a variety of combat enhancements as well as better options for traversal, mount handling, and movement. Monsters have been fine-tuned with better AI behavior, and the entire skill tree has been revamped. The game's photo mode has been expanded, and there's an all-new tutorial. Looting and quest tracking have both been reworked.

The list goes on, based on the trailer that debuted at Gamescom. It's clear that CD Projekt Red went all out for the enhanced version of the game, so the fact that much of it will be free is ridiculous. Adding free DLC to the mix is the cherry on top.

Fans are in utter disbelief. "Holy FKN shit," one Witcher 3 fan wrote on Reddit. "Free upgrade in today’s gaming world is wild," another fan wrote on YouTube.

To get the free DLC, simply visit your respective platform's digital storefront — that is, unless you're on Nintendo Switch. Unfortunately, while everyone else gets free goodies, Nintendo's port will not offer the same. There's one consolation for Nintendo fans, though: A native version of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered will soon be released on Nintendo Switch 2, alongside updates for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

articles.title: M6 and M5 Ultra Debut in Updated Mac mini and Mac Studio
articles.subtitle: We knew the M6 chip was coming, and it seemed likely Apple would produce an M5 Ultra chip, since it skipped the M4 generation for the Ultra.
articles.author: TidBITS
articles.content:
We knew the M6 chip was coming, and it seemed likely Apple would produce an M5 Ultra chip, since it skipped the M4 generation for the Ultra. But a late August release was unexpected and suggests Apple is clearing the decks before the early September announcements of new iPhone and Apple Watch models.

In a trio of announcements, Apple unveiled the M6 and M5 Ultra chips, revealed new Mac mini configurations with the M6 and M5 Pro, and raised the Mac performance ceiling with new Mac Studio models that use the M5 Max and M5 Ultra. The new Macs are available for pre-order now, with deliveries promised for 22 September 2026. We’ll see if Apple has predicted demand accurately enough to meet that promise for everyone who pre-orders.

I’ll admit that my eyes glazed over somewhat when I read these Apple chip and Mac announcements because there are so many picky details surrounding performance. If a friend who uses the Mac but doesn’t care about the details asked me about the changes, I’d say, “Everything is faster, but also more expensive.” For those who want the specifics, let’s dive in.

M6 and M5 Ultra

The M6 chip is the latest update in the evolution of Apple silicon. It’s the first chip to use a 2-nanometer process. Although that’s more of a marketing term than anything, chips using a 2-nanometer process can be faster and more power-efficient than those relying on a 3-nanometer process, as the M3 through M5 did.

Internally, the M6 features a “larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170 GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.” That’s two more CPU and GPU cores than the M5, a single 16-core Neural Engine, and 10% more memory bandwidth.

The “CPU complex” is interesting. Previously, M-series CPUs differentiated between “performance” and “efficiency” cores, but with the M5, Apple renamed its highest performance cores from “performance” to “super. ” Then, in the M5 Pro and M5 Max, Apple introduced a new “performance” core that sits between “super” and “efficiency” cores.

The super cores focus on single-threaded performance, the performance cores handle multithreaded workloads, and the efficiency cores manage everyday background tasks.

The M6 has 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores, whereas the M5 had 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores. Apple isn’t specifying how much faster the M6 is than the M5 in single-threaded super-core tasks, beyond saying it’s the “world’s fastest.” However, it’s 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance. Rather than repeat Apple’s benchmarks in running text, here’s a chart (thank you, Claude) that will give you a better sense of how the M6 compares to the M5 and the much older M1.

The M5 Ultra, Apple’s most powerful chip ever, comes with other architectural innovations. As with previous Ultra generations, the M5 Ultra combines two M5 Max chips, but since they’re dual-die chips, the result is Apple silicon’s first quad-die architecture. (The M3 Ultra connected two single-die M3 Max chips.

) There’s no practical benefit to users in a quad-die architecture, but it’s a huge win for Apple. The larger the die, the more difficult and expensive it is to manufacture because a defect can ruin the entire die. Dividing the design into smaller dies can substantially improve manufacturing yield and reduce costs.

The M5 Ultra’s specs are insane. It has an up-to-36-core CPU with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores, an up-to-80-core GPU, a 32-core Neural Engine, a more capable Media Engine, and support for up to 512 GB of memory with 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth. The M5 Ultra dispenses with efficiency cores entirely, devoting all CPU resources to super and performance cores. Here’s another performance comparison chart with numbers pulled from Apple’s announcement.

Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro

Look at Apple hopping on the AI bandwagon with this press release headline: “Apple’s new Mac mini, featuring M6 and M5 Pro, delivers a massive leap in AI performance, supercharging the leading desktop for always-on agentic computing.” Or just use it as a normal Mac like the rest of us.

Remember what I said about “faster, but more expensive?” Here’s where that starts. The M6 model of the Mac mini compares extremely favorably to the previous M4 model, and those with older Mac mini models will see even more performance gains. Have another chart.

Want more performance yet? For that, you’ll need a Pro chip, but since the M6 just debuted, the next best option is the M5 Pro. Apple provides no comparisons between the M6 and M5 Pro, but based on previous generations, the M5 Pro should substantially outperform the M6 in multithreaded and GPU-intensive tasks, even though the M6 is newer. Here’s how it compares to the M4 Pro and M2 Pro models.

The only other changes are connectivity improvements: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and upgraded 2.5Gb Ethernet with a 10Gb option available. Those come thanks to Apple’s N1 wireless chip, which also adds Thread support. (Note that the M6 Mac mini supports Thunderbolt 4, whereas the M5 Pro version has Thunderbolt 5.)

That’s the faster. How about the more expensive? You’ll remember that Apple raised the price of the Mac mini several months ago (see “ Apple Raises Prices for Many Products,” 26 June 2026), with the base M4 model jumping from $599 to $799 and the M4 Pro model increasing from $1399 to $1599. Both new releases add $100 to the price, so the M6 Mac mini starts at $899 and the M5 Pro starts at $1699.

articles.title: It’s Tim Cook’s last week on the job. Let’s review his career
articles.subtitle: Macworld Congrats to Tim Cook on his 15-year anniversary as CEO of Apple! Here are some balloons and a gift card to the Olive Garden. There will be cake in the break room.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Congrats to Tim Cook on his 15-year anniversary as CEO of Apple! Here are some balloons and a gift card to the Olive Garden. There will be cake in the break room.

It occurs to this furry observer that this is his last column before Tim Cook steps down as CEO of Apple. Hard to believe. The sad truth is that pretty soon we won’t have Tim Cook to kick around anymore. Other than the fact that he will still be working for the company, just in a different capacity, and we will absolutely still have him to kick around.

Still, it’s worth reviewing Cook’s tenure as Apple CEO. Apple loves it when you write reviews, right? So let’s get into it!

The Macalope’s not going to focus on politics. Apparently, there are some people who do not like it when the Macalope discusses politics.

That wouldn’t stop the horny one in any way from talking about it (it might even encourage him), but he thinks he’s already been clear about his feelings on Cook’s recent forays into the political world and Cook hasn’t done anything of late to really get the antlers itching, if you know what the Macalope means (you don’t and you do not want to). The Macalope has no idea what Cook’s personal politics are.

He suspects they probably pretty much align with his own. Cook’s business politics, however, would best be driven out to a rural town and gently tipped into an underground coal fire, never to be seen again.

So, it’s a little rich (allusion intended) when the Macalope sees things like this:

I hope that people say I was a good and decent man. And if they say that at the end of the day, I feel like I have achieved something. Apple CEO Tim Cook (CBS News interview, August 13, 2026)

I hope that people say I was a good and decent man. And if they say that at the end of the day, I feel like I have achieved something.

Mmm. Sorry, Tim. You might need a time machine for that.

But let’s just look at Cook’s legacy as a simple CEO running a small business in downtown Cupertino.

If you’re an Apple investor, it’s hard not to think of Cook as one of the greatest CEOs of all time. The Macalope’s not going to bother to look it up and figure it out with stock splits and buybacks and all the free coffee distributed and t-shirts shot out of a canon at shareholders meetings, but if you invested 15 years ago when Cook took over, you have to be happy with the returns.

(Hilariously, 15 years ago is about exactly when the Macalope sold the two (2) shares of Apple stock he owned.)

As someone who regularly had to deal with nincompoops who continued to say Apple was going to go out of business long after it made a lick of sense, the Macalope owes Cook a personal debt of gratitude for finally making it clear that that was not a thing you could say anymore and be taken seriously by anyone.

Despite the insistence of many that Apple hasn’t released any truly great products since Steve Jobs died, Apple has actually released some truly great products since Steve Jobs died. Sure, none of them have been as world-changing as the iPhone, the greatest consumer electronics product of all time, but, you know, that’s a pretty high bar. The Apple Watch, loudly declared a flop for years, is everywhere, as are AirPods, and Apple TV continues to churn out hit shows and movies.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Tarae: The Unbound is an 'Eastern dark fantasy' action RPG, and I for one am here for K-Diablo
articles.subtitle: Featuring one of my favorite ARPG class archetypes: Guy With Gun.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
It brings me no joy to admit this, but recently I've begun thinking that I'm finally nearing my fill of ARPGs. I've gotten a lot of great years out of clicking a mouse button and exploding full screens of skeletons, but the prospect doesn't quite spark joy like it used to.

Or at least that's what I thought until roughly 45 minutes ago, when I saw the announcement trailer for Tarae: The Unbound that had been slipped into a Gamescom 2026 Opening Night Live Montage.

The problem, I now realize, is that I've mostly spent my time with ARPGs looking at the same kinds of things. Most games downstream of Diablo tend to flow into the same basin of interchangeable demons, dark cultists, and piles of weird meat. But looking at the brief clips of Tarae, I realize now I'd just been aching for a jolt to the ARPG aesthetic palette.

Developed by Boundary and published by Krafton, Tarae's Steam page says it's set in "a world that reimagines Eastern myth, folklore, and traditional aesthetics, where beauty and mystery are entwined with darkness and brutality." It shows in the listings screenshots and embedded gifs, where enemies are being fought in Buddhist temples and player characters are battling bosses with hauntingly distended features plucked from East Asian monster illustrations.

If that's not enough, Tarae: The Unbound also includes one of my favorite character class conceits: Just an old guy with a matchlock gun. Although this particular handgunner seems to know something I don't about how historic firearms work, because he's able to pump out rapid fire gouts of firebomb explosives. Good for him.

From the sounds of it, Boundary is aiming to offer a variety of buildcrafting systems: "The balance and conflict of the Five Elements, the harmony of Yin and Yang, karma and the cycle of reincarnation all shape your leveling, equipment, and combat style," the developer says. "Even within a single class, different choices lead to entirely different builds."

I can't begin to guess how that will all work in practice, but I'm eager to experience our K-Diablo future when the time comes. It likely won't be for a bit, however: Tarae: The Unbound doesn't have a release date, unlike the full release of Path of Exile 2 now pegged for December 11, but you can wishlist it on Steam now.

iPhones

Apple replaces text labels with symbols

articles.title: Best Thunderbolt and USB-C docking stations for your MacBook 2026
articles.subtitle: Macworld Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop. We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.

Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C

The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.

USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps

USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps

Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.

While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.

The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).

The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.

For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer.

Add external displays to your MacBook

If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk.

Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac.

You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI).

Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac.

DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: AAPL stock slides, but is it a reaction to AI announcements?
articles.subtitle: There’s been an unusually large drop in the price of AAPL stock so far this week, losing roughly $25 per share in the two days since the WWDC keynote.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
There’s been an unusually large drop in the price of AAPL stock so far this week, losing roughly $25 per share in the two days since the WWDC keynote.

While some are inevitably speculating that investors weren’t impressed by Apple’s AI announcements, there are other factors at play …

Yahoo Finance was one of those to attribute the slide to the WWDC announcements.

Apple Inc shares were down 4% on Tuesday afternoon after the company’s annual developer conference left some investors questioning the pace of its artificial intelligence rollout, even as analysts broadly viewed the event as a step forward […] Despite the reported improvements, analysts flagged meaningful limitations.

Siri AI will launch in beta later this year for supported devices set to English and will not be available initially in the European Union on iOS or iPadOS. The feature is also excluded from China due to regulatory hurdles. That leaves two markets which, together, account for roughly 35% of trailing 12-month iPhone shipments, according to Morgan Stanley.

Other commenters, however, pointed to broader macroeconomic factors affecting a range of stocks, not just AAPL.

US stock futures declined on Wednesday after the US launched “self-defense strikes” against Iran in response to the downing of an American helicopter, escalating tensions in the region. Investors also awaited the release of US inflation data for fresh signals on the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook, after stronger-than-expected jobs figures last week reinforced expectations of an interest rate hike before the end of the year.

There are also suggestions that investors are selling some existing holdings in order to participate in the SpaceX IPO.

articles.title: Everything We Saw At Gamescom Opening Night Live
articles.subtitle: This year’s Gamescom just kicked off with another Opening Night Live showcase hosted by Geoff Keighley. We knew a few games that would be making an appearance in advance, like Final Fantasy VII Revelation and the new expansion for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt,...
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
This year’s Gamescom just kicked off with another Opening Night Live showcase hosted by Geoff Keighley. We knew a few games that would be making an appearance in advance, like Final Fantasy VII Revelation and the new expansion for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, but those two games cannot fill a two-hour show, so there was a lot more to see. If you didn’t get a chance to watch the show live, you can watch the VOD below, or keep scrolling for all the highlights.

Nodusfall

Kicking things off is a new dark fantasy game from Genshin Impact developer Hoyoverse called Nodusfall. If you’re looking for the company’s typical anime-inspired gacha game, you will not find it here. Instead, you get something that looks similar to a FromSoftware game. The game will feature cooperative play in which groups of four coordinate to take down powerful monsters.

Rainbow Six Tactics

Ubisoft is up next with a new entry in the Rainbow Six series, but instead of a shooter, it’s a tactical game similar to XCOM. You can make up a squad of returning Rainbow Six operators, then carefully plan and execute their infiltration into enemy territory. The game will launch next year.

Gears of War: E-Day

The Coalition was here with Gears of War: E-Day, which host Geoff Keighley made a point of emphasizing is an “Xbox console exclusive.” Almost as if that might’ve been part of the deal to get the game on stage as Xbox tries to rebrand as a company that cares about exclusives. Anyway, the story trailer shows what definitely looks like a Gears of War prequel. Buff people be yelling. Oh damn, aged-down Marcus Fenix is kind of uncanny. Anyway, the game’s coming to PC and Xbox Series X/S on October 6.

Ananta

NetEase showed off a new look at its anime-expired sci-fi/ GTA -like game Ananta. It’s got a lot going on. It’s launching on January 15 on PC and PS5, and will be free-to-play.

Silent Hill: Townfall

Konami shared a new trailer for Silent Hill: Townfall highlighting some of the acting talent in the game, as well as the spooky shit fans will have to face when it launches on September 24.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy

Next up is a new look at Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, which is coming out in two days on August 27.

Sea of Remnants

Sea of Remnants is a pirate game that combines elements of Tomb Raider with a turn-based RPG. It’ll be free-to-play and is taking preregistration requests on its official website.

Crimson Desert Enhanced

An updated version of Crimson Desert called Enhanced is out now, featuring new story moments and all post-launch updates thus far.

articles.title: Apple's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter Expands to More Countries
articles.subtitle: Alongside the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac mini models, Apple today expanded its 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max to Vietnam and countries in Europe that use the type C two-pin Europlug.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Alongside the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac mini models, Apple today expanded its 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max to Vietnam and countries in Europe that use the type C two-pin Europlug.

The updated variant of the power adapter has a retractable two-prong design. The prongs pop back into the power adapter's enclosure, making it easier to tuck into a bag or a pocket. Apple previously debuted a standard U.S. variant in September 2025 alongside the iPhone 17 models, and a type G plug version in November 2025.

Countries where the type C 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max is available include Austria, Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, and Vietnam. In most eurozone countries, it's priced at €45.

The 40W Dynamic Power Adapter is the same size as Apple's 20W charger, but it offers faster 40W charging. It also supports up to 60W charging in short bursts to speed up charging further. The power adapter can fast charge ‌iPhone 17‌ models, the iPhone Air, and the iPad Pro models.
